name: Long take
summary: A shot that runs for minutes with no visible cut; the camera and the actors carry the scene and the viewer sees real time.
how: Plan the take in blocks of 2 to 10 minutes; the length of a reel or a memory card sets the limit.
Hide a needed cut in a dark surface, a door, a wipe past a wall or a digital stitch, and keep it under 0.5 seconds.
Move the camera at a steady pace and let the actors enter and leave the frame so that the framing changes by itself.
Rehearse each move to a few centimetres, because a mistake at minute eight spoils the full take.

origin.note: Alfred Hitchcock shoots Rope in takes of about 10 minutes, the length of one reel, and hides each join in a dark back or a close shape.

adoptions.via: Orson Welles opens Touch of Evil with a single crane and tracking shot of about three minutes.
Béla Tarr cuts Sátántangó into 150 shots in 7 hours, many of them takes of several minutes.
Alexander Sokurov makes Russian Ark as one Steadicam take of 96 minutes through the Hermitage.
Birdman, shot by Emmanuel Lubezki, hides its cuts to look like one take.
1917, shot by Roger Deakins, joins a few long takes into the look of one shot.

sources.title: David Bordwell, The Way Hollywood Tells It (University of California Press, 2006)
